sec.title: Background
sec.p: Primary Immune Regulatory Disorders (PIRDs) are caused by genetic defects resulting in diverse clinical manifestations. We aimed to present the spectrum of PIRDs in children in Kuwait.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: The data was obtained from the Kuwait National Primary Immunodeficiency Disorders Registry (KNPIDR), and the patients were followed prospectively.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: 59 patients with PIRDs, constituting 14% of all patients registered in the KNPIDR, were included in this study. Most of the patients belonged to familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis syndromes (42.4%), followed by regulatory T cell defects subcategories (15.3%). The median ages at the onset of symptoms and diagnosis were 4 and 18 months, respectively. Parental consanguinity was documented in 88.1% of cases while family history of PIRDs in 45.7%. The most common clinical features were lymphoproliferation, hematologic manifestations, and infections, affecting 71.2%, 67.8%, and 47.5%, respectively. Genetic diagnosis was reached in 84.9% of the tested patients and the most common genes affected were STXBP2 followed by PRF1 and LYST. Most patients (88.8%) had autosomal recessive disease. 35.6% of the patients underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation and a similar percentage received immunosuppressive and/or immunomodulating therapies. There was a total of 21 deaths (35.6%) with a median age at death of 36 months while the median time from diagnosis to death was 5 months.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: PIRDs are heterogenous group of disorders with complex disease phenotypes. Genetic testing should be done as soon as possible when these diseases are suspected since early diagnosis is crucial for proper therapeutic interventions.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Primary Immune Regulatory Disorders (PIRDs) are a subgroup of Inborn Errors of Immunity (IEIs) characterized by heterogeneous clinical phenotypes, which are not distinct to specific diseases. This can lead to delays in diagnosis and initiation of treatment, hence genetic testing is crucial for achieving an early diagnosis and management of PIRDs [1]. The International Union of Immunological Societies Expert Committee (IUIS) 2022 update describes more than 500 IEI-associated genes, with 72 of these (14.17%) are categorized as PIRDs causing genes [2]. The genes identified to cause PIRDs were divided into 7 subgroups: Familial Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (FHL syndromes), FHL syndromes with hypopigmentation, regulatory T cell defects, autoimmunity with or without lymphoproliferation, immune dysregulation with colitis, autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome, and susceptibility to EBV and lymphoproliferative conditions [2].

PIRDs are caused by pathogenic genetic variants that lead to defects in the immune system, leading to different mechanisms for disease development and immune dysregulation. These mechanisms were recently reviewed and include but not limited to decreased NK cells and CTL activities, regulatory T cells defects, actinopathies, IL10 deficiency or unresponsiveness, apoptosis defects, and defect in negative selection of autoreactive T cells in the thymus [2–6].

The Middle East and North Africa region (MENA) have high rates of consanguineous marriage ranging between 20 and 50% with increased the prevalence of IEI [7, 8]. A recent report from the MENA region showed that among 5871 patients genetically evaluated, the majority (65.2%) had autosomal recessive (AR) defects [9]. Another report showed a similar pattern where 76% of 2457 molecularly confirmed IEI cases had AR mode of inheritance [10].

Treatment of PIRDs patients especially with long term complications is challenging, usually initiated with steroids and immunosuppressants. However, because of their long-term side effects and associated infections, targeted immunotherapies, such as cytokine or small molecule inhibitors, are increasingly available and more favorable with fewer immunosuppressive effects. Allogeneic Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) can be considered as curative therapy if PIRDs patients do not respond to immunosuppressants and targeted immunotherapies [6, 11].

The current study aimed to present the spectrum of PIRDs in children in Kuwait during the period of 2004 to 2024. This will hopefully highlight the importance of this group of diseases and help physicians with early diagnosis and timely management.

sec.title: Data
sec.p: The data was obtained from the Kuwait National Primary Immunodeficiency Disorders Registry (KNPIDR) [12], as part of a study approved by The Research and Ethics Committee of the Ministry of Health in Kuwait, and by the Kuwait University Health Sciences Center Ethical Committee, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Informed written consent was obtained from patients and/or families for whom testing was done for research purposes. The extracted data included patients diagnosis, demographics, ages at onset of symptoms and diagnosis, clinical manifestations, genetic variants, treatments, outcome, and cause of death, We also recorded the dates of diagnosis, HSCT, and death. The patients were followed prospectively, and they were categorized according to the diseases of immune dysregulation table of the International Union of Immunological Societies (IUIS), Primary Immunodeficiency Diseases Committee Report on Inborn Errors of Immunity (2022) [2].

sec.title: Inclusion Criteria
sec.p: The inclusion criteria included all children (0–14 years) with PIRDs and registered in the KNPIDR during the period 2004 to 2024. Patients were diagnosed with PIRDs if they satisfy at least one of the following: (a) the presence of a pathogenic variant in a gene implicated in PIRDs [2], (b) clinical diagnosis of FHL based on the HLH-2004 diagnostic guidelines [13], (c) have a disease phenotype of immune dysregulation with no identified etiology (e.g.: infection, connective tissue disease, malignancy) [14].

sec.title: Genetic Variant Interpretation
sec.p: Variant interpretation was based on the guidelines of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) and the Association for Clinical Genomic Science (ACGS) [15–17]. Sequencing reads were aligned to the human reference genome (GRCh37) using BWA, and variant calling for single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and small insertions/deletions (indels) were performed using GATK with standard hard filtering parameters. Copy number variants (CNVs) were classified according to the joint recommendations of ACMG and the Clinical Genome Resource (ClinGen) [15].

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: The study cohort included 59 patients with PIRDs with almost equal number of males and females (30 and 29 patients). They constitute 14% of all patients registered in the KNPIDR. Most of the patients belonged to FHL syndromes (42.4%), followed by regulatory T cell defects subcategories (15.3%) (Fig. 1; Table 1). Four patients (6.8%) were labeled as other immune dysregulation since they did not fit into a specific subcategory (inclusion criteria c). The median follow-up time per patient was 68.8 months [Interquartile range (IQR) 6.2-164.6]. The median age at onset was 4 months (IQR 1–27), and the median age at diagnosis was 18 months (IQR 2.5–70.5). The median time for delay in diagnosis (defined as the time from first clinical sign suggestive of PIRDs to the time of actual diagnosis) was 4 months (IQR 1–26). Parental consanguinity was documented in 52 patients (88.1%), while a positive family history of PIRDs was reported in 27 cases (45.7%). Three patients (22, 40 and 43) were screened and diagnosed due to family history of the disease. The diagnosis was made for patients 22 and 40 soon after birth while patient 43 was diagnosed at the age of 36 months and continued to be asymptomatic and received HSCT at the age of 42 months.

sec.title: Clinical Manifestations
sec.p: Clinical manifestations were analyzed across the cohort of the 59 patients (Table 1; Fig. 2). The most common clinical features included lymphoproliferation in 42 patients (71.2%), hematologic in 40 patients (67.8%), and infections in 28 patients (47.5%). Conversely, the least frequently reported findings were malignancy (Hodgkin’s lymphoma) in 1 patient with FAS deficiency (1.7%), and atopy in 3 patients (5.1%), highlighting their rarity in this cohort of PIRDs. The low prevalence of malignancy in our cohort could be due to the need for a longer follow-up period.

caption.p: The frequency of different system involvement in the clinical presentation of 59 patients with PIRDs registered in the KNPIDR

sec.p: Autoimmune manifestations were identified in 15 patients (25.4%) within the cohort, highlighting the integral role of immune dysregulation in disease expression. The most frequently observed autoimmune conditions included thrombocytopenia (7 patients), anemia (6 patients), and thyroiditis (4 patients), followed by vitiligo and autoimmune enteropathy. Diagnostically, autoimmune features were most commonly associated with AIRE deficiency (4/4 patients), LRBA deficiency (3/3 patients), and immunedysregulatory disorders not otherwise classified (3/4 patients). Additional cases were noted in Fas deficiency (2 patients), with isolated instances reported in FASLG deficiency, SOCS1 deficiency, and FOXP3 deficiency.

sec.title: Genetics
sec.p: Genetic testing was done for 53/59 patients (89.8%) and a molecular diagnosis was reached in 45/53 patients (84.9%) (Table 1). This means that 8/53 patients (15%) had genetic testing done but no defects were found. The total number of patients in our cohort with no molecular diagnosis was 14/59 patients [23.7%, (10 patients were diagnosed with FHL and 4 patients were diagnosed as other immune dysregulation)]. Four out of the 10 FHL patients with no molecular diagnosis underwent genetic testing for the FHL causing genes using Sanger Sequencing, but no pathogenic variants were found. The most common genetic diagnosis identified was STXBP2 deficiency, diagnosed in 7 patients followed by PRF1 and LYST deficiency, diagnosed in 5 patients each. The mode of inheritance in the patients with genetic diagnosis was AR: 40/45 patients (88.8%), X-linked (XL): 4/45 patients (8.8%), and autosomal dominant (AD): 1/45 patient (2.2%).

sec.title: Treatments and Overall Outcome
sec.p: All patients with FHL were treated with HLH-2004 protocol. Among all patients included in this study, 21 (35.6%) underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), with a promising survival rate of 81%, as 17 patients were alive at last follow-up (Table 2). The median duration of follow up post-HSCT was 109.1 months (IQR 41.3-165.4). The diagnoses of patients who underwent HSCT included: STXBP2 deficiency (FHL5) (n = 4), FHL (n = 4), LYST deficiency (n = 3), FASLG deficiency (n = 2), STX11 (FHL4) (n = 2), RAB27A deficiency (n = 2), PRF1 deficiency (FHL2) (n = 2), FOXP3 deficiency (n = 1), and XIAP deficiency (n = 1).

sec.p: There was a total of 21 deaths (35.6%) among the study cohort. The most common diagnosis among the deceased patients was FHL (n = 7), followed by STXBP2 deficiency (FHL5) (n = 3), and LRBA deficiency (n = 3). Other diagnoses included PRF1 deficiency (FHL2) (n = 2), immune dysregulation disorder (n = 2), and one patient each with FASLG deficiency, LYST deficiency, RAB27A deficiency, and TNFRSF9 deficiency. The median age at death was 36 months (IQR 7-152) while the median time from diagnosis to death was 5 months (IQR 2–14). Sepsis was the most common cause of death, reported in 14 patients, followed by pulmonary hemorrhage in 5 patients. Additionally, pneumonia and aspiration pneumonia were each responsible for one death.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: PIRDs are important forms of IEI that need special attention due to complexity and severity in clinical presentation. 14% of all patients registered in the KNPIDR were diagnosed with PIRDs compared to a mean frequency of 8.5% among all IEI patients reported from several MENA countries [1], 6.2% among patients registered in the European Society for Immunodeficiencies Registry [18] and 3.8% in the United States Immunodeficiency Network (USIDNET) Registry [19]. This is most probably caused by the high frequency of consanguineous marriages in our population compared to other populations and observed in 88% of the presented patients. This is clearly evident in our study as almost 90% of the reported patients have an AR disease. We should emphasize that the true number of patients with PIRDs in Kuwait during the study period is most likely more than the reported ones since many patients may either expired before diagnosis or remain undiagnosed.

Our cohort is characterized by an early onset of symptoms (median 4 months) and a significant delay in diagnosis (median 4 months). This signifies that there is lack of awareness among pediatricians about when to consider PIRDs among the differential diagnoses. Pediatricians should be educated that PIRDs are multi-system diseases, and patients may present with diverse manifestations specially lymphoproliferation, hematologic, autoimmunity and /or unexplained fever.

The results clearly demonstrate the critical role of genomic testing in establishing a definitive diagnosis, which is essential for guiding appropriate treatment strategies in patients with PIRDS. Identifying the causative pathogenic variants also enables effective prevention of recurrence through preimplantation or prenatal genetic diagnosis. Moreover, it facilitates cascade screening of at-risk family members, an especially valuable approach in the Kuwaiti population, where approximately 50% of marriages are consanguineous [20]. It is important to note that most of the variants reported in this study have been previously published, with supporting evidence from both segregation and functional analyses [21].

Given the severity and complexity of PIRDs, treatment strategies often require intensive and multifaceted approaches. This highlights the critical importance of timely intervention and personalized treatment in improving outcomes for patients with these potentially life-threatening disorders. The reported patients were treated with a range of immune modulatory and suppressive therapies like systemic steroids and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and several patients received more targeted biologic agents tailored according to the underlying genetic diagnosis. 35% of the patients in our cohort were treated with HSCT as curative therapy, which is similar to the percentage of patients registered in the USIDNET [19]. The overall survival of our transplanted patient was 81%. It is higher than a recent report from the Primary immunodeficiency Treatment Consortium (PIDTC), which reported an overall survival of 67% [22]. However, a careful reading of the PIDTC report shows that it included a wide range of patients with IEI who had immune dysregulation manifestations like combined immunodeficiencies, common variable immunodeficiencies, autoinflammatory and innate immune defects. Unfortunately, outcome studies for HSCT in PIRDs as a group are currently lacking. We should highlight that supportive care measures, such as antimicrobial agents, nutritional support, and management of organ-specific complications, are essential additions to therapy.

Interestingly, the frequency of deaths (35.6%) and the death ages in the current study is similar to our previous study that we published 14 years ago and included patients with PIRDs [23]. This means that the healthcare gaps, which include physicians’ awareness about PIRDs and IEI in general were not addressed effectively during this period.

In conclusion, PIRDs are heterogenous group of disorders with complex disease phenotypes. Early diagnosis is crucial for proper therapeutic interventions. Genetic testing, preferably going directly to the whole exome / genome sequencing (WES / WGS); should be among the first-tier investigations when evaluating patients with multi-system manifestations. The therapeutic approach in these patients necessitates an individualized, multidisciplinary strategy guided by genetic findings, disease trajectory, and transplant eligibility, with a goal of preventing irreversible immune-mediated damage and improving survival.
